chunks: Safe LiPo charging rate limits. The question: How fast can you safely charge a LiPo?
A lithium cell has a maximum safe charging current, and it is usually written as a multiple of its capacity (a C-rate). For most cells it is about 0. 5C to 1C.
Charging faster than the cell can absorb makes metallic lithium plate onto the anode, which is permanent damage, and it also makes extra heat. The datasheet limit is the rule.
Imagine pouring water into a bottle with a narrow neck. Pour slowly and everything goes in. Pour too fast and water splashes over the sides.
Lithium ions going into the graphite behave like that. If they arrive faster than they can slip in, they pile up on the surface as metal.
Unlike spilled water, the plated metal does not come back.
The solid curve is the real total time; the dashed hyperbola is the naive 60 over C minutes.
They converge at low rates, but beyond about 1C the gap is a CV tail that does not shrink. Going from 1C to 4C saves only about 29 minutes while the CC heating is 16 times larger.
The 4C point in the model is nearly all CV because the cell hits 4. 2 volts almost at once.
C-rate: the charge current divided by capacity. 1C on a 2 Ah cell is 2 amps ("What a LiPo C rating means").
Anode: the negative side of the cell, made of graphite, which soaks up lithium during charging. Lithium plating: lithium turning into metal on the anode surface.
Cold, high current and a nearly full cell make it worse. Fast-charge cell: a cell built and rated for more than 1C charging.
I²R heat: heat that grows with the square of the current ("Battery internal resistance").
Charge time: total time to full, which does not shrink in step with current because of the CV tail ("When LiPos charge fastest").
Charge a 2 Ah cell with 50 milliohms of internal resistance. At 1C the current is 2 amps, and the heat is 2 squared times 0. 05 equals 0. 2 watts.
At 2C the current is 4 amps, and the heat is 4 squared times 0. 05 equals 0. 8 watts, four times as much. Yet the total charge time only drops from about 77 minutes to about 54.
The extra stress buys little, which is why most designs stay near 0. 5C to 1C. That is the whole idea.
"For a standard LiPo the safe charge rate is about 0. 5C to 1C, so 1 to 2 amps for a 2 amp-hour cell. Some cells are rated for 2C or more, but the datasheet is the limit.
The constraints are lithium plating, which gets worse at low temperature and high state of charge, and I squared R heating.
Faster has diminishing returns, since 2C only saves about 30 percent of total time versus 1C, so I charge at 1C or below within about 0 to 45 degrees, with current-based termination."
